summary:
Colombia's formal legal framework is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

That framework sits alongside lethal, targeted violence. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands before drowning in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín; her mother Sandra Borja stated "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. The El País report of 14 April 2025 noted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals, stating "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announced cleansing of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots", threatening a further wave of "social cleansing"; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. The Guardian reported more than 40 transgender women killed in Colombia in 2023.

The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience as killings rise.

A Colombian court has protected the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty in a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees, and a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup. The 2016 Ministry of Interior presidential decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict; a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. The 2016 government decree specifically addresses LGBTI rights in health care.

Discrimination based on sexual orientation has carried one to three years' imprisonment plus fines since a 2011 law. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed: the "Inconvertibles" bill of Congressperson Mauricio Toro, introduced 10 May 2022, had failed by 2024, and Congressperson Carolina Giraldo proposed the similar bill "Quiérele siempre" in 2025. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS at Universidad de los Andes, recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilization as a prerequisite for other physical changes.

Access to public and commercial facilities has been protected by court order, citing judgment T-314 of 2011 on the Tequendama Hotel, judgment T-909 of 2011 on Cosmocentro mall's guardianship officials and security firm, and judgment T-301 of 2004 on Santa Marta police at the boardwalk. The Constitutional Court extended social security benefits to same-sex couples on 5 October 2007 and pension rights on 17 April 2008. In 2012 the Court found that sexual orientation cannot be a criterion for preventing blood donation. Since 2014 LGBTQ individuals can adopt their partner's biological child, the 4 November 2015 ruling granted full same-sex adoption rights barring agency discrimination, and a 12 November 2015 ruling required birth registration listing two mothers or two fathers.

Colombian society remains generally conservative despite supportive media coverage. A bloc of conservative senators defeated the civil union bill in Congress on 19 June 2007, and by 31 March 2016 a campaign to force a referendum repealing the November 2015 same-sex adoption ruling had gathered 1.8 million signatures including 45 members of Congress, though a Congress committee shelved it 20 to 12 in May 2017. An Invamer poll of October 2019 put same-sex marriage support at 50% against 47% opposed, and adoption at 36% in favour against 62% opposed.
tangentialFactors:
The Attorney General's Office count of 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025 and the Guardian's figure of more than 40 transgender women killed in 2023 are raw counts without population denominators; they do not by themselves establish Colombia's per-capita risk relative to other jurisdictions, and Colombia's decades-long armed conflict inflates baseline homicide levels generally.

Armed-group "social cleansing" campaigns in Guajira and Caquetá name trans and gay people explicitly alongside drug users and sex workers, indicating that in those departments the threat is driven by non-state armed actors rather than by ordinary criminality or by state policy.

The July 2023 Special Jurisdiction for Peace indictment of 15 former rebels for gender persecution as a crime against humanity is a transitional-justice proceeding tied to the conflict; its findings concern past conduct by demobilised combatants rather than current state enforcement.

Trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, a route available since June 2015 without medical examination; national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Discrimination based on sexual orientation carries one to three years' imprisonment plus fines under the 2011 law. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed as of 2025, with the "Inconvertibles" bill having failed by 2024 and the "Quiérele siempre" bill proposed in 2025.

A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a separate court ruling protected the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty.

Same-sex couples have had social security benefits since 5 October 2007 and pension rights since 17 April 2008. Sexual orientation cannot be used to prevent blood donation under a 2012 Constitutional Court ruling. Adoption rights were granted in stages: since 2014 LGBTQ individuals can adopt their partner's biological child, the 4 November 2015 ruling granted full adoption rights barring agency discrimination, and a 12 November 2015 ruling required birth registration listing two mothers or two fathers.

In 1998 the Constitutional Court ruled that public school teachers cannot be fired for revealing their sexual orientation and that private religious schools cannot ban gay students from enrolling. After student Sergio Urrego's suicide in August 2014, the Constitutional Court ordered the Ministry of Education to review the manuals of coexistence of all schools nationwide so that they contain no articles discriminating against children by sexual orientation or gender identity.

Bogotá and Medellín have gay neighbourhoods, bars and counselling and legal advice centres. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS at Universidad de los Andes, recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilization as a prerequisite for other physical changes.
outOfScopeNotes:
The claim that national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, and the 1993 Constitutional Court jurisprudence on self-recognition without surgical requirement, appear in the prior summary but are not present in this source inventory; they are retained for continuity but are not independently verifiable from the sources supplied here.

The inventory does not state whether the June 2015 notary route for changing the sex marker remains the operative procedure as of 2026, nor whether the November 2025 "trans" and "non-binary" markers are available on passports as distinct from national ID cards.

No source in this inventory documents airport or border-screening treatment specific to trans travellers, nor any entry or visa rule keyed to gender presentation or document markers; those questions are unresolved here.

The 13 trans people killed in Q1 2025 (El País) and the 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025 (Attorney General's Office) cover different populations and periods and cannot be reconciled into a single rate from these sources; no per-capita or general-homicide denominator is provided for either figure.

The most recent documented incident in this inventory is the Millerey killing of 5 April 2025 and the Guajira and Caquetá flyer campaigns; no later incident is documented here, and the absence of a later record does not establish that such violence has ceased.
